readings.title: Fresh produce after the market closes
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A town market closed before many workers finished their shifts. Stallholders wanted unsold vegetables to reach local families instead of becoming waste. The central difficulty was a short collection window after closing. The first collection time worked for daytime volunteers but excluded many people who could help in the early evening. The organizers knew that a tidy plan in an office might not match what happened in an ordinary week.

The group first tried two weeks of collection records. Sellers noted what remained each day, while volunteers recorded arrival times and whether vegetables could be moved safely. They therefore listened to people who used the place at different times, including those who seldom attended formal meetings.

The trial showed later pickups reached more helpers. On several days the amount available was small, so sending a vehicle every evening would not have been efficient. In response, the group adopted a flexible pickup and message system. The group arranged collection only when sellers reported enough food and invited volunteers from several shifts to respond. The notes did not remove every disagreement, but they made the reasons for the next decision easier to explain.

The broader lesson was clear: food recovery depends on timing as well as goodwill. A generous aim became practical only when the group matched available food with people who could collect it safely. Keeping a record of small changes also helped the team distinguish a temporary setback from a lasting problem. For the people involved in fresh produce after the market closes, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: Making a cafeteria label useful
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A workplace cafeteria listed ingredients beside each dish. Managers thought the list answered questions about meals, but some customers remained uncertain. The central difficulty was labels that were difficult to compare quickly. The ingredient print was small, and different dishes used different terms for similar foods; a crowded lunch line gave little time to read. A first impression was not enough to tell the whole story, because different people approached the service in different ways.

The group first tried a simpler label trial beside three dishes. Staff used clear headings and consistent terms, then watched whether customers could find the information they needed without asking. The team compared comments with direct observations rather than assuming that the loudest opinion represented everyone.

The trial showed consistent wording reduced repeated questions. A few diners still needed individual advice, reminding staff that a label cannot answer every personal dietary concern. In response, the group adopted larger text and a contact point for questions. The cafeteria revised its boards and made a trained staff member available for details that did not fit on a short sign. Some suggestions were inexpensive, while others would have required a change to staffing or equipment.

The broader lesson was clear: information should be usable in its real setting. The team judged labels by how they worked during a busy lunch, not by how complete they looked on an office screen. The final proposal remained open to revision when new information became available. For the people involved in making a cafeteria label useful, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: Learning to cook with limited equipment
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An evening course taught inexpensive meals to adults living in small flats. The first recipes assumed everyone owned an oven and several pans. The central difficulty was recipes that required unavailable kitchen tools. Participants described shared kitchens, limited storage and irregular work hours; these details mattered as much as the price of ingredients. Several participants valued the original aim even though they questioned the first method chosen to reach it.

The group first tried a one-pan cooking session. The tutor prepared a meal using basic equipment and asked learners to identify steps that would still be difficult at home. Short conversations after the activity revealed details that a written form had failed to capture.

The trial showed preparation time was a larger barrier than cost. Several learners could buy the ingredients but could not complete a complicated meal after a late shift. In response, the group adopted short recipes with optional steps. The tutor reduced preparation stages and offered suggestions for adding vegetables when learners had more time or equipment. The people responsible made their limits clear and invited others to describe any unintended effects.

The broader lesson was clear: practical teaching begins with learners’ conditions. A recipe is helpful only when it can be prepared in the kitchen and time that a learner actually has. This approach gave the group a practical basis for its next round of work. For the people involved in learning to cook with limited equipment, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

readings.title: A walking group changes its pace
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A community health centre offered a weekly walking group. Early posters called it an easy walk, yet several newcomers did not return. The central difficulty was an unclear promise about walking pace. Experienced members moved quickly, and some participants felt unable to ask the whole group to slow down. The project began on a small scale so that its organizers could learn before making a permanent commitment.

The group first tried a conversation with new walkers. The leader asked what parts of the route felt comfortable and which moments made people unsure about joining again. They noted both benefits and costs, including the time that volunteers or staff needed to give.

The trial showed short rests mattered more than distance. The route length was acceptable for many walkers, but a continuous pace made the activity feel demanding. In response, the group adopted two pace options and planned rest points. Volunteers marked clear meeting places and allowed walkers to choose a shorter loop without explaining personal health details. The public summary described what had changed and what questions had not yet been answered.

The broader lesson was clear: inclusive activities need clear choices. A group can keep its social purpose while making different levels of participation visible and easy to choose. Readers could therefore judge the decision by its evidence rather than by a promise of perfect results. For the people involved in a walking group changes its pace, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly. This careful pace mattered: people were more willing to support a decision when they understood which observations had shaped it and which concerns remained.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A market may have food left at closing time even while nearby families would welcome it. Moving that food safely requires more than goodwill. Sellers need to know what can be collected, and volunteers need enough time to arrive before the food loses its freshness. A town group kept simple daily records and found that the available amount changed greatly from one evening to another. It introduced a message system so that a collection trip was made only when there was enough to justify it. The group also invited helpers who could work after daytime jobs. By matching supply with realistic schedules, the project reduced waste without placing an unreasonable burden on volunteers.
translation.explanation: 注意even while对比、so that目的关系和By doing方式状语。
translation.referenceAnswer: 市场打烊时可能仍有剩余食物，而附近家庭正好需要。要安全地运送这些食物，光有善意还不够。摊主需要知道哪些食物可以收集，志愿者也需要有足够时间在食物失去新鲜度前赶到。一个城镇小组保留了简单的每日记录，发现每晚可收集的数量差别很大。于是他们建立了消息系统，只在数量足以值得专程前往时才安排收集。他们也邀请白天工作后仍能帮忙的人参与。通过把供应与现实时间安排相匹配，项目减少了浪费，也没有给志愿者造成不合理负担。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to a market committee proposing how unsold vegetables could be collected and shared safely. Describe the roles of sellers and volunteers and explain how to avoid unnecessary trips.
writing.explanation: 范文覆盖安全交接、志愿者安排和减少空跑。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I suggest a short trial for sharing vegetables left at the end of market day. Sellers could send a message about the type and amount of food available before the stalls close. A coordinator would then contact trained volunteers who can collect it promptly and take it to a nearby community kitchen. Sellers should keep food in suitable containers and explain when it was prepared or displayed.
To avoid wasting volunteer time, collection should take place only when enough food is available. The team could record the amount collected, travel time and any safety concerns for four weeks. These notes would show whether the plan is useful and what needs changing. A public summary could thank everyone involved and explain the next decision.
Yours sincerely,
A local resident
